newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech govt coalition angered by opposition demands.
newsitem.headline: Czech govt coalition angered by opposition demands.

text.p: The Czech governing coalition reacted angrily on Monday to parliamentary demands made by the opposition Social Democrats directing Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's minority government to address several issues.

Last week, the Social Democrats (CSSD) attempted to push the government to implement anti-dumping legislation, submit a concept creating a pro-export policy, as well as demanding a halt to the privatisation of hospitals.
But Klaus, flanked by coalition party leaders Josef Lux of the Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL) and Jan Kalvoda of the Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA) rejected CSSD's moves to govern through parliament.

"The basic criteria of the relation betwen the cabinet and parliament is the programme declaration. Any other political methods of influencing the executive -- above the constitution -- we consider to be unacceptable," a coalition statement said.

The tersely-worded statement added that the coalition was ready to respect the role of the opposition, but "at the same time, (we) call for the opposition to do the same, that means to respect the government".
It said that on these issues, there was no dissent among the coalition parties, which have in the past have not always been united.

In July, the government passed its agenda through parliament, but only after prolonged negotiations with the CSSD, giving its leader Milos Zeman, a long-time rival of Klaus, the key position of parliamentary speaker.

The CSSD, which walked out of the programme vote allowing the agenda to be approved, made strong in-roads in June elections, denying the coalition of its previous majority by one seat in the 200-seat Chamber of Deputies.
The two leaders have had several run-ins over the past few weeks, as the political climate heats up with a key battle over the 1997 budget and November Senate elections looming on the horizon.
On Thursday, Klaus issued a virulent attack on Zeman who emerged as power broker after the elections and whose tacit support is crucial to the survival of the minority government.
Klaus accused the Social Democrats of joining forces with the other opposition parties, the Communists and ultra-right Republicans, to try to reverse the post-Communist reforms he has led.

Klaus said the post-electoral agreement with the Social Democrats did not mean he had signed on to some form of "puppet government". Zeman replied in kind saying the legislature would not be a "puppet parliament."

Elections to the Senate will be the first test of the new alignment of political forces since the elections to the lower house deprived Klaus's coalition of its majority and made the Social Democrats the second biggest political party.
A poll released on Monday by the private firm Factum showed the CSSD had surged past the ODS in voter preference leading up to the first round of voting scheduled for November 15-16.
The survey showed 24.4 percent of respondents support CSSD Senate candidates, while 23.7 percent would vote for ODS under a first past-the-post system in 81 constituencies.
It is the first time since pre-Senate election polls began in July that the CSSD has led the ODS.
